title: In R[z]/(z^p-f) in characteristic p, p-th powers lie in R and each prime of R has exactly one prime over it
statement: Let $p$ be a prime number and $R$ an integral domain with $p=0$ in $R$. Let $f\in R$ and let $C=R[z]/(z^p-f)$ be the quotient of the polynomial ring $R[z]$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring] by the ideal generated by $z^p-f$; assume that $C$ is an integral domain. Then: (1) the ring map $R\to C$ is injective and $C$ is integral over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]; (2) for every $c\in C$ the element $c^p$ lies in the image of $R$; (3) for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$ there is exactly one prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset C$ whose inverse image in $R$ is $\mathfrak p$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07PR (lemma-helper-G-ring, line 12306), proof: 'for every element of B or C some power of it lies in A. Hence there is a unique prime ... lying over p', for the step B subset C = B[z]/(z^p-f); clause (3) from (1), (2) is Algebra, Lemma Tag 0BR8 (lemma-powers, algebra.tex line 10718) with the lying-over Lemma Tag 00GQ (lemma-integral-overring-surjective) used in its proof

proof.text: (Clause (1).) Write $\varphi:R\to C$ for the structure map and $\bar z$ for the class of $z$ in $C$. The polynomial $z^p-f\in R[z]$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring] is monic of degree $p$, so by [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free] the ring $C=R[z]/(z^p-f)$ is a free $R$-module with basis $1,\bar z,\ldots,\bar z^{p-1}$; in particular it is a finitely generated $R$-module. The map $\varphi$ is $r\mapsto r\cdot1$, and $1$ is a member of this basis, so $r\cdot 1=0$ forces $r=0$: $\varphi$ is injective. Since $C$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, $C$ is integral over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral].

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07PR (lemma-helper-G-ring), proof: 'Set C = B[z]/(z^p - f) and note that B subset C is finite'

proof.text: (The Frobenius is additive in $C$.) Since $p=0$ in $R$, also $p\cdot1=\varphi(p\cdot 1)=0$ in $C$. Let $x,y\in C$. By the binomial formula in the commutative ring $C$, $(x+y)^p=\sum_{k=0}^{p}\binom pk x^ky^{p-k}$. For $0<k<p$ the prime $p$ divides $\binom pk$: from $\binom pk\,k!\,(p-k)!=p!$, $p$ divides the right side, and $p$ divides neither $k!$ nor $(p-k)!$ (products of integers between $1$ and $p-1$), so, $p$ being prime, $p\mid\binom pk$. These terms are therefore $0$ in $C$, and $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$. By induction on the number of summands, $(x_0+\cdots+x_m)^p=x_0^p+\cdots+x_m^p$ for all $x_0,\ldots,x_m\in C$; and $(xy)^p=x^py^p$ by commutativity.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07PR (lemma-helper-G-ring), proof: 'Set C = B[z]/(z^p - f) and note that B subset C is finite' (the power property of C over B, which the source derives from the pure inseparability of L/M; written here directly)

proof.text: (Clause (2).) Let $c\in C$. As $C$ is a quotient of the polynomial ring $R[z]$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring], $c$ is the class of a polynomial, $c=\sum_{i=0}^m\varphi(b_i)\bar z^i$ with $b_i\in R$. By Step 2, $c^p=\sum_{i=0}^m\varphi(b_i)^p(\bar z^p)^i$, and $\bar z^p=\varphi(f)$ in $C$ because $z^p-f$ lies in the ideal divided out. Hence $c^p=\varphi\big(\sum_{i=0}^m b_i^pf^i\big)$ lies in the image of $R$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07PR (lemma-helper-G-ring), proof: 'Set C = B[z]/(z^p - f) and note that B subset C is finite' ('for every element of B or C some power of it lies in A')

proof.text: (Clause (3), at most one prime.) Let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ be a prime ideal and let $\mathfrak q,\mathfrak q'\subset C$ be prime ideals with $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q')=\mathfrak p$. Let $c\in\mathfrak q$. By Step 3 there is $r\in R$ with $c^p=\varphi(r)$. Then $\varphi(r)=c^p\in\mathfrak q$, so $r\in\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q')$, so $c^p=\varphi(r)\in\mathfrak q'$; since $\mathfrak q'$ is prime, $c\in\mathfrak q'$ (if $c\notin\mathfrak q'$, then $c^n\notin\mathfrak q'$ for all $n\ge1$ by induction on $n$). Hence $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak q'$, and by symmetry $\mathfrak q'\subseteq\mathfrak q$, so $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak q'$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0BR8 (lemma-powers), proof, first paragraph (injectivity on spectra, then surjectivity by Lemma Tag 00GQ)

proof.text: (Clause (3), existence.) By Step 1 the map $\varphi:R\to C$ is injective and $C$ is integral over $R$. By lying over [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-lying-over], every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$ is the contraction $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$ of some prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset C$. With Step 4, for every prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R$ there is exactly one prime $\mathfrak q$ of $C$ with $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$.
